1: In March 1954 a letter arrived at a cottage outside a village in the North Riding of Yorkshire, addressed to A. Hepburn, and it had been written by a fourteen-year-old girl in Lancashire who had just seen a film. The woman who opened it was called Agnes Hepburn. She was sixty-one years old, she had taught in a village school for thirty-four years and had retired the previous summer, and she had never been to a cinema in her life. The letter ran to three pages. It asked whether it was frightening to be looked at by that many people, and it said that the girl's mother had died in January, and it asked, near the end and in a different handwriting as though it had been added later, whether things got easier. There was no return address on the envelope, only on the last page, written small, as though the girl had decided about it late. Agnes read it twice. Then she did the thing that she would go on doing for twenty-two years, and that nobody asked her to do, and that she never once described as a kindness. She wrote back. She explained, in the first paragraph and without coyness, that the letter had come to the wrong Hepburn, that she was a retired schoolmistress and not an actress and had no connection of any kind to the person intended. She gave the correct address in London, in full, so the girl could send it again. And then, at the bottom of the page and running over onto a second one, she answered the question about whether things get easier, which took her most of an afternoon and which she later said was the only part of the letter she had found difficult.
2: The postal error was not mysterious and was not rare. There was an agency in London handling the actress's correspondence, and it employed a rotating staff of young women working from an address book, and A. Hepburn in Yorkshire had been entered into that book in 1952 by somebody who was doing three things at once and was gone from the job within the year. Nobody checked it, because the letters that went astray never came back and so nothing ever looked wrong from the London end. Roughly one letter in every forty went the wrong way, which does not sound like much until you know the volume: between 1954 and 1976 about nine hundred letters arrived at the cottage. Agnes answered every one, in the same order every time, and the order is the whole of her method. First she said plainly that the letter had come to the wrong person. Second she said, if the letter had said anything about the writer's own circumstances, that she was sorry about it or glad about it as appropriate. Third she gave the correct address of the agency in London, every time, in full, so that the writer could send it again. And fourth — and this is the part that turned an administrative error into whatever this actually was — if the letter had asked a question that a person could answer, Agnes answered it herself, at length, as herself. The four steps never varied. Her nephew, going through the archive in the nineteen-nineties, said that you could pick up any reply from any year and know within two lines where you were in the sequence, and that after a while this stopped seeming mechanical and started seeming like the point.
3: She was not pretending to be anybody. This has to be said clearly because it is the first thing people assume and it is the opposite of what happened. Every surviving reply — and about two hundred and forty survive, because people kept them — opens with some version of the same sentence, and several of them open with exactly this one: I am not the person you meant to write to, and I am going to tell you how to reach her, but I have read your letter. There was no deception and there was no game. What there was, instead, was an old woman with a great deal of time, a lifetime of practice at reading what a child is actually asking underneath what a child has written down, and a professional objection to leaving a question unanswered. She said once, to her nephew, that in thirty-four years of teaching she had never met a question worth ignoring and had met a great many adults who ignored them, and that as far as she could tell this was the main thing that was wrong with the world. She was also, by every account, not especially warm. Two of her former pupils described her in almost identical terms decades apart: exacting, dry, impossible to charm, and the only adult in the village who treated a child's question as a real question rather than as a noise a child makes. Neither of them used the word kind and both of them said they would have gone to her with anything. That combination is rarer than the warm version and is probably what made the letters work, because a fourteen-year-old can tell the difference between being comforted and being answered, and only one of those is any use in January.
4: The letters were not what people imagine either. A small number were about the films, and those Agnes could do nothing with and said so, cheerfully. The overwhelming majority were about the writer. They were from girls between about twelve and nineteen, mostly, and they asked about things that have nothing to do with cinema: whether you are allowed to want to leave the place you were born, what to do about a father who has stopped speaking to you, whether being plain matters as much as everyone says it does, how to know if you are actually any good at the thing you like doing. One in 1961, from a girl of sixteen in Glasgow, consisted of a single sentence and a signature. Agnes's reply to it ran to five pages. The girl in question, who is now in her eighties, has said publicly that the reply was the first time an adult had written to her as a person, and that she has no idea whether the advice in it was good, and that this has never seemed to her to be the relevant question about it. What the single sentence said, she has never disclosed, and she has been asked repeatedly. She will say only that it was a question, that it was the sort of question a sixteen-year-old asks once and then never asks again if the answer goes badly, and that Agnes Hepburn took it entirely seriously. There is a second pattern in the letters that the archivists noticed and that nobody has explained. The proportion asking about leaving home rises sharply after 1963 and stays high, and the proportion asking about appearance falls by roughly half over the same period. Agnes's replies track the change without ever remarking on it.
5: About a third of them wrote back. That is the fact that turns this from an anecdote into a correspondence, and it is the thing Agnes herself found most surprising. They had the agency's address by then. They had been told exactly how to reach the person they meant to reach. And roughly one in three chose to go on writing to the schoolmistress in Yorkshire instead. Several said openly in their second letter that they had sent the original to the agency as instructed and received a signed photograph, and that they were writing to Agnes because they wanted an answer rather than a photograph. The correspondence with the girl from Glasgow lasted nineteen years. The one with a woman who first wrote in 1957 from Belfast, at seventeen, was still going in 1976 and by then had survived a marriage, two children and an emigration to Canada. Agnes never met any of them. It was offered several times — one woman proposed driving up from Birmingham, another asked whether she might visit while passing through on holiday — and Agnes declined every offer, always politely and always without giving a reason. The nephew thought the reason was obvious and unsentimental: a letter can be answered properly, and an afternoon in a front room cannot. There is also the possibility, which he raised and did not settle, that she did not want to be looked at — that a woman who had spent twenty years being the most useful correspondent in several hundred lives had a fairly clear idea of how ordinary she would appear in a doorway, and preferred the arrangement in which that did not come up.
6: It cost her money, and this is worth putting a number on because it is the least sentimental thing in the story and the most convincing. Agnes Hepburn lived on a teacher's pension. Nine hundred replies, most of them several pages, many of them to addresses abroad, over twenty-two years, at the postage rates of the period, came to a sum that her nephew — who went through her accounts after she died and who was not a sentimental man either — worked out at somewhere between four and five per cent of her total income across that entire period. She bought paper in bulk. She had a standing order with a stationer in Northallerton. In 1968 she wrote to that stationer to query a price increase and the letter survives and it is, by a distance, the sharpest thing in the whole archive. She was not a saint and would have been irritated by the suggestion. She simply held the view that a letter is a thing somebody has made and sent, and that not answering one is a small act of contempt. There is one more figure worth having. In 1971, at seventy-eight, she had a fall and spent five weeks in hospital in Northallerton, and she had the current stack brought in to her, and she answered thirty-one letters from the ward. The hospital notes record her asking twice for more paper. Her handwriting in those five weeks is visibly worse and the replies are not shorter. One of the thirty-one was to a girl in Cardiff who had written about a brother who had gone to prison, and it runs to seven pages, and it was written in a public ward by a woman of seventy-eight with a broken hip. It is the longest reply in the entire archive.
7: The actress found out in 1976. Exactly how is not clear and the two accounts disagree; the likelier one is that a woman who had corresponded with both of them mentioned it in a letter to the agency, and somebody there finally looked at the address book and understood what had been happening for twenty-two years. The entry was corrected within the week. That, on its own, would have ended the story, and it nearly did. What happened instead is that in the autumn of that year Agnes Hepburn, then eighty-three, received a letter from Switzerland. It was handwritten and not long. It said that the writer had learned only recently what had been going on, that she had spent some time trying to work out whether to be embarrassed and had concluded that the question was not about her, and that she understood a number of people had been answered properly who would otherwise have received a photograph. It thanked her for that specifically and without any flourish. And it asked, at the end, whether there was anything the writer could usefully do. It was signed with a first name only. Agnes's nephew, who read it in 1978 and again in 1994, said the striking thing was not the letter's warmth, which he had expected, but that it contained no offer of money, no proposal to publicise anything, and no request of any kind — and that in his experience of correspondence from people in that position, all three of those absences were unusual. The letter had evidently been written without help: there is a crossing-out in the second paragraph and a word inserted above the line, which does not survive a secretary.
8: Agnes replied by return, and her reply is the last document in the archive, and it is four sentences long. She said that there was nothing to thank her for because she had not been doing it for anybody's benefit, including her own. She said that the letters had never really been about the person they were addressed to, and that she suspected the recipient had worked that out some years before she had. She said that the only thing anybody could usefully do was answer the post. And then she said that she was eighty-three and would be stopping soon in any case, and that she hoped the agency had hired somebody sensible. She died in 1978. The nephew kept the box. It went to a county archive in 1994, and the woman from Glasgow and the woman from Belfast, who had never met and did not know the other existed, both travelled to see it in the same year, eleven months apart. The archivist who dealt with both visits, and who did not connect them until afterward, said that each of them asked to see the same thing first, which was not their own file. Both asked whether it was true that there had been nine hundred. The archivist told both of them the same thing: that the figure is an estimate and the real number is probably higher, because the cottage had no filing system and Agnes threw away the incoming letters once she had answered them. Only the replies survive, because the people who received them decided, separately, that they were worth keeping. This story is a work of fiction. Agnes, the agency, the archive and every detail in it are invented, created for storytelling and not drawn from any record.
